payload.text: The amber light flattens as Tamsin Vale, Brother Odo, and Kestrel come down to the ford. The ferry sits chained against the far bank, patient and useless. The ferry-house door gapes on its hinge. Inside, the mooring rope ends in a clean, high cut, a yard off the floor. The strongbox lies pried open and empty on its side. Small clawed tracks cross the dust and lead out the back toward the causeway, then down into the reeds, where the river swallows the trail. No bell sounds. No birds call. Only the water, loud and indifferent, and somewhere above the rafters, the faint creak of old boards settling — or something shifting its weight.

payload.body: Tamsin Vale, Brother Odo, and Kestrel arrived at Greyhollow Ford to find the ferry chained uselessly to the far bank. The ferry-house stood open. Inside: the mooring rope cut cleanly a yard above the floor, the strongbox pried open and emptied. Small clawed tracks crossed the dust and led out the back toward the causeway, then into the reeds where the trail vanished. No bell rang. No birds called. Only the river's indifferent roar and the faint creak of something shifting weight in the rafters above.
payload.title: The ferry at Greyhollow Ford lies sabotaged

payload.body: The mooring rope was cut by something with claws—possibly small, possibly not (the tracks are small, but the cut is high and clean, suggesting tool use or leverage). The strongbox was emptied; contents unknown. A second presence in the rafters, moving deliberately. The bell's silence is deliberate: the rope cut prevents ringing. Reed-camp location: southwest into the marshland.
payload.title: DM: Unknown intruder with claws, unknown accomplice in rafters

payload.text: Where am I standing exactly?
I look around to clue me into where I am standing. A boat? The shore?

Planks underfoot, not deck boards — Tamsin stands inside the ferry-house itself, the river's slap muffled through stilted floor. The cut rope hangs at chest height just ahead, frayed ends pale against the dark hemp. To the right, the strongbox gapes empty on its side. Behind her, the front door still swings on its hinge toward the ford; ahead, the back door stands open on the timber causeway, running off into the reeds where the chained ferry waits, useless, across the water. Above, the boards creak again, closer to the loft's edge than before.

What does Tamsin do with that creak still settling overhead?

payload.body: Tamsin Vale stood in the ferry-house, surrounded by signs of sabotage: the bell-rope cut cleanly, the strongbox emptied and overturned. The chained ferry lay useless across the water. Something moved in the loft above—boards creaking under slow, deliberate weight, drawing closer to the edge. The back door opened onto a timber causeway running into the reeds.

payload.text:
Tamsin crouches to the toppled strongbox and runs her hands through it — splinters, dust, the cold absence of coin. Nothing but air and old rust, until her fingers catch on the hinge: a knot of netting wedged there, green reed-twine twisted through torn cord, marsh-made, goblin-made. She holds it up just as the loft above goes silent — not settling now, but still, deliberately still, the way something goes quiet when it knows it's been heard.

Brother Odo's breath catches. Somewhere above, dust sifts down between the boards.

What does Tamsin do with the loft gone quiet above her?
Easy now... *hums three soft notes* Friend up there — we've no wish for blood. Shiny trinkets buy more peace than steel ever has.
I hold up my holy symbol where the loft can see it glint, and speak low: we mean no harm, and have trade to offer if it comes down in peace.

payload.body: Tamsin Vale searched the toppled strongbox in the ferry-house and found it empty of coin but caught with her fingers a knot of green reed-twine—goblin-made, marsh-work—wedged in the hinge. As she held it up, the loft above fell deliberately silent. Brother Odo heard it too. Something up there knows it's been discovered.
payload.title: The bell-ringer's mark at Greyhollow Ford

payload.text: Who is there?
Let's be cautious
I shout "Who is there? Reveal yourselves!"

Tamsin's voice cracks up through the boards, sudden and loud enough to make Brother Odo wince. For a heartbeat nothing answers but the river's slap under the stilts — then the loft erupts with motion. A woman drops half into view at the hatch-edge, gaff hook thrust out before her in both hands, knuckles white, eyes wild over the rim of it. "Stay back — stay back, I'll gut the lot of you!" Her gaze flicks from Tamsin to Odo's glinting symbol to Kestrel, voice fraying. "You from the reeds? You bring my boy back?"

What does Tamsin say to Wenna, hook still leveled at her chest?
Oh— no, good woman, no goblins here, only tired travelers. We've seen no boy, but we'll help you look, by the Mother's own promise.
She's no goblin — put the symbol away, Tamsin. Fear needs gentler coin than trinkets now.

payload.body: At Greyhollow Ford, Tamsin's shout drew out a woman named Wenna from the ferry loft, gaff hook brandished and voice breaking. She demanded to know if the party came from the reed-camp, asking if they had her boy. Brother Odo stood witness to her fear and the river's current below the stilts.
payload.title: The ferry loft holds a desperate woman

payload.body: Wenna cut the bell line herself when her son did not return from the reeds at nightfall. She has been in the loft alone since then, waiting.
payload.title: dm: The ferry bell was silenced—Wenna's doing

payload.text: We have seen no boy. What happened here?

Wenna doesn't lower the hook, but something in her shoulders gives, like rope paying out under strain. "Three days now," she mutters, then catches herself and says it plain. "Dusk-fall, three nights back — small shapes, quick as eels, up the sunk-timber walk from the reeds. Took the strongbox. Took my clapper-bell. Took my Pell." Her eyes go wet and furious at once. "Counted him three times before I believed it, counted the steps after 'em till the mud swallowed the tracks." She studies Tamsin, hook trembling. "You'll bring him back? Swear it on the old water, and maybe — maybe I'll show you a way through the reeds."

What does Tamsin swear to her?

payload.body: Wenna the ferryman admits the bell was taken three nights ago at dusk-fall. Small quick shapes came up from the reeds along the sunk-timber walk—took the strongbox, the clapper-bell, and her son Pell. She counted him three times before believing he was gone, then tracked them into the mud until the trail vanished. She offers to show a way through the reeds if Tamsin swears by the old water to bring Pell back.
payload.title: Wenna's grief at Greyhollow Ford

payload.text: I swear by the gods I will find your boy, Pell. Show us the way and we will bring him home.

Wenna's shoulders drop like a cut line. The gaff hook sags, then clatters to the boards, and she presses the back of her wrist to her mouth, counting breaths under it — three in, three held. "On the old water, then," she says, rough. "Old water don't forget a promise." She wipes her face and jerks her chin toward the hatch, toward the dark water beyond the stilts. "Sunk-timber walk's the only dry way through the reeds. Follow close. Third span's rotted clean through — step wrong there and every ear in the marsh will know you're coming."

She looks to Tamsin, waiting.

How does Tamsin lead the party out onto the causeway?
Goblins post a lookout high up — reeds won't hide us from that.

payload.body: Tamsin Vale swore to Wenna that she would find Pell, the ferryman's lost boy, and bring him home. Wenna accepted the oath by the old water's measure. Her grief gave way to practicality: she sent the party toward the hatch and the dark water beyond the ferry stilts, directing them onto the sunk-timber walk—the only dry passage through the reeds to reach the reed-camp. She warned of a rotted third span that would betray their approach to every ear in the marsh if they stumbled.
payload.title: Wenna's oath and the sunken-timber walk

payload.text: Kestrel, what do you suggest? How can we spot the Goblins before they spot us?
I'll go ahead low through the reeds and watch the high ground — if there's a lookout, I spot him before he spots us.
I scout ahead along the sunk-timber walk, scanning treelines and high points for a goblin lookout before the others move.

Kestrel slips ahead onto the sunk-timber walk, weight low and even, skirting the black gap where the third span has gone soft with rot. Reeds hiss and part around her, a heron croaking once and falling silent. She goes still near a tilted post where the walk bends toward higher ground — and there, strung between two stakes above the waterline, hangs a leather strap, slack and swaying, the bell long gone from it. Nothing stirs nearby. No goblin shape breaks the reeds, no eyes catch hers.

What does Kestrel do now?

Patience, Kestrel - count three breaths before you move again. No sense waking what's sleeping.

payload.body: Kestrel crept ahead along the sunk-timber walk toward the ford, moving low past the rotted third span. A heron startled and fell silent. She found the bell—or what remained of it—strung between two stakes above the waterline on its leather strap, now empty and slack. No goblin guard was visible in the reeds nearby. The bell itself is gone.
payload.title: The bell at Greyhollow Ford has been cut down

payload.text: What did you see Kestrel?
Bell's gone from its strap — cut loose, not fallen. No eyes on me yet, but that proves nothing with a lookout posted.
Don't go glinting anything till I find their watcher, Odo — that's a good way to end up with an arrow in your eye.

Kestrel's voice carries low across the water. "Bell's gone from its strap — cut loose, not fallen. No eyes on me yet, but that proves nothing with a lookout posted." Behind her the strap sways on its stakes, its cut edge pale against old leather. Wenna's hand tightens on the rail, counting breaths again. The light is nearly spent now, the sky gone the color of a bruise, and the river's voice has risen to fill the silence where the bell should hang. Ahead, the sunk-timber walk narrows toward the rotted third span, black water showing through its broken ribs.

What does Tamsin do, with the dark closing in and the crossing still ahead?

payload.body: Kestrel reports the ferry bell severed deliberately—not fallen. The strap swings empty on its stakes, cut edge pale. She warns the party to keep metal hidden; a lookout is posted somewhere in the gathering dark. The sky has turned bruise-colored and the ford's crossing remains blocked as full dark approaches. The rotted timber walk ahead narrows toward a broken third span.

The group moves as one behind Wenna, boots finding the drier timbers by memory of her lantern-swing. Odo and Kestrel match her hush step for step, breath held, symbols and bowstrings dark and still. But the rotted span catches Tamsin's heel — a crack splits the quiet like a dropped plate, and somewhere off in the reeds a startled voice yelps too loud to be anything but a boy's, quickly smothered. Smoke drifts thin over black water, and on a low mud island ahead, firelight flickers against a bare pole where a clapper once hung.

payload.text: We take the ferry back home

Pell's rag glows red in the ferry-house window long before they reach it, Wenna already on the porch with a lantern that shakes worse than her voice. "Three hours," she snaps, counting it under her breath like a curse, "three hours I've had that boy telling me goblins and bells and you lot still out in the black water—" but her hands are already pulling Pell into her apron, already reaching past him for Tamsin's wrist. She throws the ferry-house door wide, drags a coiled rope up from a strongbox that smells of brine and old coin, presses it into Tamsin's arms. "Old water carried him home. Carry yourselves the same."

The cut rope waits at the dock, and the far bank is close enough to throw for.
Bronze found, boy safe, rope near enough to mend — the marsh gave back more than it took tonight. But Tamsin, stand still a breath, you're white as the clapper and bleeding where you don't notice.
I set a hand on Tamsin's arm and tend her wounds — binding what's torn, murmuring the old three-note hymn under my breath to steady my own hands as much as hers.

Odo's hand finds Tamsin's arm before she can wave him off, and he works fast by lantern-light — tearing a strip from his sleeve, winding it tight over the worst of the torn skin, his three-note hymn barely more than breath. It steadies his own fingers more than it steadies the wound. He ties off the binding and lets his hand fall away. Wenna's lantern throws long shadows across the dock, the coiled rope heavy in Tamsin's arms, the cut end of the old line waiting a yard short of the far bank.

Throw it before the dark finishes what the goblins started — I'd rather not swim for it.
